events.content: Stage 'ratification_landscape' begins
Weak labor enforcement keeps Democrats opposed and stalls the deal.
Democratic and union pressure to reopen the deal for enforceable labor provisions builds each round.
Media scrutiny of the stalled deal grows.

Discussion so far:
  us_congress_dem: Look, the agreement as written doesn't have a mechanism — it's commitments on paper. My members won't vote yes on that. We need Mexico to accept independent labor inspections and real consequences, or we reopen the deal. That's the only path to 218 votes.
  business_lobby: Look, I hear you — your members won't vote blind. Here's the play: we don't reopen the whole deal. Mexico adds independent inspection panels and real consequences for non-compliance. That's workable, that's fast, and that gets us to 218. Dragging this into a full renegotiation costs us six months and kills every investment commitment we've made.
  labor_union: Independent panels work — but "real consequences" has to mean facility-level inspections, rapid access, and automatic tariff response if Mexico blocks them. No delays, no political carve-outs. You want us at the table with Democrats? That's the condition.
  us_congress_dem: Look, I'm not going to soften this: independent panels are useless if Mexico can delay inspections or Mexico's government shields factories from access. We need automatic consequences—tariffs kick in 30 days after a blocked inspection, full stop. That's what gets labor and Democrats to yes.
  canada_domestic: Before we go further: are you talking a bilateral protocol with Mexico on inspections and tariffs, or are you reopening the whole agreement? Because if it's the latter, Canada's dairy terms and Chapter 19 are back on the table—and that's not happening. I need to know the scope before I can move.
  mexico_gov: Okay—bilateral labor protocol, Mexico-U.S. only, no reopening USMCA. Canada stays out, your dairy terms stay locked. But automatic tariffs on inspection delays? That's not enforcement, that's economic coercion. We'll accept independent panels, real access, and consequences—but Mexico decides the remedy, not Washington. That's the deal.
  trade_lawyer: Here's what I think works: Mexico pre-commits—in writing, in the protocol—that if inspectors are blocked or delayed past 15 days, tariffs trigger automatically on a pre-set list. Mexico doesn't "decide the remedy"; it pre-authorized the consequence. That's not Washington coercion, that's Mexico's own rule. Can you live with that framing, or are we genuinely stuck on who holds the trigger?
  mexico_gov: No—pre-committing to automatic tariffs is the same coercion dressed differently. Mexico accepts independent panels and real access, yes. But the remedy comes through dispute resolution, not a timer. We enforce our own labor laws; you don't impose consequences for how we do it.
  media_actor: Congressman, real talk: if Mexico won't accept automatic tariffs, even pre-authorized, does your caucus have any room on a third-party enforcement mechanism—like a joint commission with binding arbitration and escalating remedies that *don't* start with tariffs? Or is the tariff trigger genuinely non-negotiable for 218 votes?
